## Motivation {.smaller}

**Every time you open a new AI chat, it starts from scratch. I built a fix.**

::: {.incremental}
- **The Problem**: You spend the first ten minutes re-explaining your project, your preferences, your decisions. The session ends. Next time, you do it all again. The model is smart — but it has no memory.
- **Why not enterprise tools?** Solutions like RAG exist, but they require a learning curve, ongoing costs, and debugging skills most individuals don't need. You wouldn't rent a warehouse to store a notebook.
- **The Spark**: A conversation with Professor Vincent about markdown note-taking — three months ago — sent me down a rabbit hole. I went home that night and started building.
- **The Result**: The **Neural Vault** — a structured Obsidian vault that gives the AI persistent context. No database. No infrastructure. Just markdown files and a simple workflow.
:::

::: {.notes}
Start by asking the room: "Has anyone here ever had to re-explain yourself to an AI that should already know you?"

That's the problem. Every time you open a new Claude or ChatGPT session, the model has no memory of you. You're starting from zero — every single time. The model itself is incredibly capable. The bottleneck isn't intelligence. It's context.

Now, enterprise solutions exist — things like RAG and vector databases. But think of it this way: you wouldn't rent a warehouse to store a notebook. These tools have a learning curve, they cost money, and when they break, they're hard to fix. For one person, that's too much overhead.

Three months ago, I was in a conversation with Professor Vincent about markdown files and note-taking — and something clicked. I went home and started building. The result is the Neural Vault: a structured set of plain text files that you paste into Claude at the start of every session — so it already knows who you are, what you're working on, and what you've already decided.

No cloud. No API. No setup beyond installing a free app.
:::

## The Obsidian Brain Preview {.smaller}

**Your knowledge, connected and readable by both you and the AI.**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
<br>

- **Inbox**: Raw capture — quick, unorganized thoughts.
- **Wiki**: Structured knowledge the AI helped you write.
- **Archive**: Deprecated notes, kept for history.
- **Agent Sandbox**: A messy workspace for AI agents — kept separate so your vault stays clean.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
![](obsidian_graph.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
So what does the vault actually look like? This is a preview of the structure.

On the right you can see the Obsidian graph view — every dot is a note, and the lines between them are links. This is what your knowledge looks like when it's connected.

On the left, the four main folders. The Inbox is where you dump quick thoughts — anything you want to capture fast without worrying about formatting. The Wiki is the polished layer — structured notes that the AI helped you write and that you've reviewed. The Archive is for anything outdated — you don't delete notes, you retire them. And the Agent Sandbox is a dedicated messy space for AI-generated drafts and experiments, kept separate so your clean vault stays clean.

The key insight is that every one of these files is plain text — markdown. That means any AI can read them. You don't need a special plugin or connector. You just paste the file into the chat.
:::

## Where the Brain Idea Came From — and What It's Missing {.smaller}

**The `Meta/About_Me.md` tells the AI who you are. Karpathy had the same idea — but solved a different half.**

:::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](aj_karpathy_thinking.png){width="100%" fig-align="center" style="border-radius: 8px; max-height: 280px; object-fit: cover;"}
<div style="font-size: 0.72em; color: #64748b; text-align: center; margin-top: 4px;">Two people, one problem, different solutions</div>
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **The `raw/` → `wiki/` pipeline**: Dump raw notes in; the LLM rewrites them into clean wiki pages
  <div style="background-color: #f1f5f9; padding: 8px; border-radius: 4px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.8em; margin-top: 4px; border-left: 3px solid #3b82f6;">
  **Prompt:** "Read these raw notes. Synthesize them into a structured wiki page with a summary, key concepts, and actionable takeaways."
  </div>
- **LLM-written, human-curated**: AI writes, you edit
- **Health checks**: Periodic passes to find gaps and stale notes
- **Web Clipper ingestion**: Articles auto-converted to markdown
:::

. . .

> *Karpathy solved how to **build** a knowledge base. He didn't solve how to **use** it in an active session.*
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The most important file in the entire vault is a simple text file called About_Me.md. It lives in the Meta folder. It's a few paragraphs about who you are, how you work, and what you're focused on. Every session starts by handing this file to Claude.

Around the same time I was building this, Andrej Karpathy — former head of AI at Tesla, co-founder of OpenAI — published a very similar idea. The AI community went wild for it.

His insight was elegant: instead of manually writing your notes, have the LLM do it. You dump raw material — articles, highlights, rough thoughts — into a folder. A prompt tells the AI to synthesize them into clean, structured wiki entries. You review and approve. Over time, you build a knowledge base that the AI helped write.

It's a brilliant system for ingesting and organizing knowledge from what you read.

But here's the gap — Karpathy's system tells you how to build the vault. It doesn't tell you how to use it in an active working session. How do you load it into Claude? How do you make sure the model has the right context before you start? That's what I built.
:::

## Context Injection Protocol {.smaller}

**How to load the brain into an active session.**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](two_layer_diagram.png){width="100%" fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.column width="55%" style="font-size: 0.82em;"}
::: {.incremental}
- **Two-layer memory split**: Claude holds *who you are*; Obsidian holds *what you know*. 
- **The Handshake**: A structured prompt template used at the start of every session.
- **The `About_Me.md` File**: The core of the protocol.
  <div style="background-color: #f1f5f9; padding: 8px; border-radius: 4px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.8em; margin-top: 4px; border-left: 3px solid #3b82f6;">
  # About Me<br>
  **Role:** Data Scientist focusing on predictive modeling.<br>
  **Style:** Prefer Python over R. Write concise, well-commented code.<br>
  **Current Focus:** Optimizing the customer churn pipeline.
  </div>
- **The Result**: The AI starts the session already knowing your goals, your style, and what you decided yesterday.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
So how do we actually load this knowledge into the AI? I call it the Context Injection Protocol.

The diagram on the left shows the key idea: a two-layer memory split. Layer one is Claude's native memory — the ambient stuff, who you are, your working style. Layer two is your Obsidian wiki — the technical knowledge, project decisions, session history. 

The Context Injection Protocol is the bridge. It's a structured prompt template — a handshake — that you use at the start of every session to load the right parts of your vault into the model. Not everything. Just what's relevant.

For example, you might paste in a prompt that says: "I am starting a new session. Read the attached About_Me file for my background, and Project_Spec for our current goal. Do not start working yet. Acknowledge you have read the context."

The result? The AI starts the session already knowing your goals, your style, and what you decided yesterday. You never have to re-explain yourself.
:::

## The `COMMIT:` Flag {.smaller}

**How to improve the brain as you go.**

::: {.incremental}
- **The Mid-Session Problem**: Great ideas happen in the middle of a chat, but get lost when the chat ends.
- **The Solution**: Tell Claude to mark insights worth saving.
- **How it works**:
  *"If we reach a decision or write a good piece of code, prefix it with `COMMIT:`. This is my signal to save it to my vault."*
- **Ideas Are Never Lost**: Every good session turns into a permanent note in your notebook.
- **An Investment in the Future**: The notebook you build today will make whatever AI you use tomorrow smarter and more aligned with you.
:::

::: {.notes}
Loading the brain is step one. Step two is improving it as you work.

The problem is that great ideas happen in the middle of a chat. But when the chat ends, those ideas are gone. 

The solution is something I call the COMMIT flag. In my initial instructions, I tell Claude: "If we reach a decision or write a good piece of code, prefix it with the word COMMIT."

When I see that word pop up in the chat, it's my signal. I know I need to copy that specific block of text and save it into my Obsidian vault before I close the window. Nothing gets lost.

Because of this, every good session turns into a permanent note in your notebook. You are constantly adding to your vault as you work with AI. 

And that's the real power of this system. The notebook you build today will make whatever AI you use tomorrow smarter and more aligned with you. You are investing in future you.
:::
